summaries.example: Imagine saying, “The soup is hot.” It may not be simply true or false. Maybe it is warm, so we give the statement a truth degree such as 0.6. In fuzzy logic, a statement can have any degree from 0, meaning totally false, to 1, meaning totally true. If two statements are joined with “and,” a rule tells us how to combine their degrees. Different fuzzy logics use different rules.
summaries.summary: Fuzzy logic studies reasoning about statements that are vague or imprecise. Instead of assigning only true or false, it often assigns a truth degree between 0 and 1. A compound statement gets its degree from the degrees of its parts by rules called truth functions. There are many choices for these rules. Some use the smaller of two degrees for “and,” some multiply the degrees, and others use different mathematical operations. These choices lead to different logics, including Łukasiewicz logic and Gödel–Dummett logic. The subject also has versions with variables and quantities, such as “all” and “some.” Mathematicians investigate what can be proved, what counts as a model, and whether proofs match the meaning given by the truth degrees. Fuzzy logic is also used to think about vagueness, including puzzles where many small changes seem unable to change a description but eventually do.
key_ideas: Fuzzy logic is a family of many-valued logics, not just one system.
The usual truth degrees range continuously from 0 to 1.
Different rules for “and,” “or,” “not,” and “if” create different fuzzy logics.
Some systems study vague ideas such as “young,” “tall,” or “huge.”
Mathematicians study fuzzy logics with formulas, models, proof systems, and algebraic structures.
summaries.why_it_matters: Many everyday descriptions have fuzzy edges. A person may be somewhat tall, and a number may be almost huge. Fuzzy logic gives mathematicians a careful way to represent such intermediate cases and to compare different rules for reasoning about them. It also shows that there is more than one way to build a logic for partial truth.

important_terms.definition: A way to study reasoning when statements can be partly true, rather than only completely true or completely false.
A number that represents how true a statement is. In the usual system, 0 means totally false and 1 means totally true.
A rule such as “and,” “or,” or “not” that joins or changes statements.
The idea that the value of a larger statement is fixed by the values of its smaller statements.
A rule for combining two truth degrees as a special kind of “and.” Different t-norms give different fuzzy logics.

questions_to_think_about: Should “the box is heavy” be only true or false, or can it be partly true?
If two statements are each partly true, should their “and” statement be less true?
Can a long chain of almost-true steps eventually lead to a clearly false conclusion?
Why might different rules for “and” be useful?

summaries.example: Suppose a statement P has degree 0.8 and Q has degree 0.6. Under the minimum rule, the conjunction P and Q receives degree 0.6. Under the product rule, it receives 0.48. Under the Łukasiewicz rule, it receives max(0.8 + 0.6 − 1, 0) = 0.4. These are not merely different calculations: each corresponds to a different account of how partial truth combines. The implication connective is then linked to the chosen conjunction by a residuation condition, which makes the logic mathematically coherent.
summaries.summary: Fuzzy logic is a family of many-valued logics designed to model reasoning with vague or imprecise propositions. In its mathematical form, formulas receive values in the real interval [0,1], and connectives are interpreted truth-functionally. The central operation is often a t-norm, a mathematically constrained form of conjunction. Important examples include minimum, product, and the Łukasiewicz operation. For suitable t-norms, implication is determined by residuation, and negation can be defined from implication and falsity. MTL is the basic logic covering all left-continuous t-norms. Łukasiewicz logic and Gödel–Dummett logic result from selecting particular operations and adding axioms; they differ in how conjunction, implication, and ordering behave. Other systems alter the assumptions, add truth constants, or use more than one designated truth degree. First-order fuzzy logics extend the approach to predicates and quantifiers, interpreting universal statements by infima and existential statements by suprema. The entry also examines algebraic semantics, proof theory, semantic games, and proposals connecting truth functions with reasoning about vagueness. In sorites arguments, a premise may be almost true rather than fully true, so repeated applications can gradually reduce truth without making every individual step seem unacceptable. The entry presents this as one possible fuzzy treatment, not as the only theory of vagueness.
key_ideas: Fuzzy logic extends classical two-valued reasoning by allowing degrees of truth, usually in [0,1].
Truth-functionality requires the value of a compound formula to be determined by the values of its parts.
The minimum, product, and Łukasiewicz operations produce important but different t-norm-based logics.
MTL is a general framework for logics based on all left-continuous t-norms; Łukasiewicz and Gödel–Dummett logic are important extensions or special cases.
Predicate versions assign degrees to statements about objects, while universal and existential formulas use infima and suprema.
Algebraic semantics, proof systems, and semantic games provide different ways to understand and justify fuzzy reasoning.
summaries.why_it_matters: Fuzzy logic separates several questions that classical logic tends to combine: how truth is measured, how compound statements are evaluated, and which inferences preserve full truth. This makes it a useful mathematical framework for studying imprecision and graded reasoning. It also connects philosophical problems about vagueness with formal issues such as completeness, decidability, proof construction, and the choice of semantics.

important_terms.definition: A many-valued logic in which values are commonly taken from the interval [0,1], with intermediate values interpreted as degrees of truth.
A function assigning a value to a compound formula from the values of its component formulas.
A binary operation on [0,1] that is associative, commutative, non-decreasing, and has 1 as its neutral element; it commonly interprets a strong conjunction.
The implication operation associated with a left-continuous t-norm through the condition x*y ≤ z exactly when x ≤ y implies z.
The fundamental fuzzy logic whose semantics ranges over all left-continuous t-norms.
A fuzzy logic based on the Łukasiewicz t-norm, with continuous interpretations of its connectives.
A logic based on the minimum t-norm, where comparisons depend especially on the ordering of truth degrees.
A semantics that interprets logical connectives as operations in an algebraic structure rather than necessarily as operations on real numbers.

questions_to_think_about: Does a degree of truth describe vagueness itself, uncertainty, or something else?
Why might the minimum and product rules represent different meanings of “and”?
What is gained by defining implication from a t-norm through residuation?
Can fuzzy logic avoid the sorites paradox, or does it merely offer a different analysis of it?
Why might propositional completeness fail or become much more difficult in some first-order fuzzy logics?

summaries.example: A weather report says, “The afternoon is hot,” and you give that statement a truth degree of 0.7. You also give “The afternoon is dry” a degree of 0.5. What should “It is hot and dry” mean? One fuzzy logic might use the lower number, 0.5. Another might multiply them, giving 0.35. A third might use a rule that gives 0.2. The choice depends on what the logic wants “and” to mean. Fuzzy logic studies these choices instead of assuming there is only one correct system.
summaries.summary: Fuzzy logic is a family of logical systems for reasoning with vague or imprecise claims. A statement such as “Maya is tall” may be assigned a degree between 0 and 1 rather than being forced into a simple true-or-false choice. In the standard mathematical setting, the degree of a compound statement is determined by the degrees of its parts. This is truth-functionality. The rules for the connectives are not fixed once and for all. The minimum, product, and Łukasiewicz operations are important examples of t-norms, which can interpret a strong form of “and.” A related implication operation can be obtained through residuation. MTL is the weakest major system built around the relevant class of t-norms. Łukasiewicz logic selects one continuous t-norm, while Gödel–Dummett logic uses the minimum t-norm and focuses on the ordering of values. Other systems can change assumptions such as commutativity, associativity, or the requirement that only value 1 counts as designated. The theory also develops predicate logics, where predicates receive degrees and quantifiers are evaluated using greatest lower bounds or least upper bounds. Researchers study formal proofs, algebraic models, and semantic games. A major philosophical issue is whether degrees of truth really capture vagueness. The entry discusses sorites reasoning, where repeated applications of an almost-true rule can gradually lower truth without making each step obviously unacceptable.
key_ideas: Fuzzy logic handles vagueness by using degrees of truth.
There are many fuzzy logics because different mathematical rules can govern the connectives.
The ordinary “and” and a stronger fuzzy conjunction need not behave identically.
MTL provides a general framework, while Łukasiewicz and Gödel–Dummett logic represent notable alternatives.
Fuzzy logic can be extended from simple statements to predicates, objects, and quantifiers.
The source distinguishes mathematical fuzzy logic from the broader use of fuzzy methods in engineering and computing.
summaries.why_it_matters: People often disagree about borderline cases without simply making a mistake: an object can be somewhat tall, or a claim can be nearly correct. Fuzzy logic offers formal tools for representing and reasoning about such cases. Its competing systems also teach an important lesson about logic: changing the meaning of a connective can change which arguments count as valid.

important_terms.definition: A type of logic that allows statements to have degrees of truth, often anywhere from 0 to 1, instead of only true or false.
A value showing how strongly a statement counts as true; 0 is totally false and 1 is totally true in the standard setup.
A logical word or symbol, such as “and,” “or,” “not,” or “if,” that combines statements.
A system in which a compound statement’s value is calculated from the values of its component statements.
A carefully defined operation used to model a strong form of conjunction in many fuzzy logics.
The basic fuzzy logic that considers all left-continuous t-norms rather than choosing only one.
A fuzzy logic using the Łukasiewicz operation and its associated implication.
A logic based on the minimum operation, emphasizing the relative ordering of truth degrees.

questions_to_think_about: Is a truth degree the same as a probability? Why might the source treat them differently?
When two claims are partly true, which rule for “and” seems most reasonable?
Why would a logic study several kinds of implication instead of using one familiar meaning?
How might fuzzy logic explain the difference between “almost true” and “totally true”?
What challenges arise when fuzzy logic handles statements about every object or at least one object?
